docs.title: About the Educator
docs.text: Education and mentoring have always been at the heart of this work — long before AI became a household word, and long after the hype of any particular tool fades away.

docs.title: A Career Shaped by Curiosity and Teaching
docs.text:
The path here did not begin with a job title. It began with a persistent question: how do you help people understand something genuinely complex without losing the depth that makes it worthwhile?

That question has driven everything — from early work in industry, through academia, and into the design of educational programmes that have shaped thousands of learners.

Writing, teaching and sharing knowledge have always been just as fulfilling as building technology. The two are not in tension; they are the same practice, viewed from different angles.

docs.title: Nationally Accredited Qualifications in Data Science
docs.text:
At a time when "Data Science" was not yet a common phrase, nationally accredited qualifications in the discipline were designed and delivered from the ground up.

This involved:

  • Defining what practitioners at every level genuinely need to know
  • Structuring content so that foundational concepts lead naturally to applied skills
  • Ensuring graduates could think clearly under uncertainty — not just execute a workflow
  • Collaborating with industry partners to keep programmes relevant and grounded

The result was a qualification that produced graduates who could reason about data, not just process it.

docs.title: Mentoring Across Academia and Industry
docs.text:
Mentoring is not a side activity. It is the work itself.

Over the years, students and professionals across both academia and industry have received guidance at moments that mattered: a career pivot, a difficult technical decision, a project that was not going as expected, or simply a conversation about what to do next.

A guiding principle

The best mentoring does not give people answers. It gives them better questions.

docs.title: Spanning Both Worlds
docs.text:
A career that moves between academia and industry creates an unusual vantage point. Academic rigour matters. So does the practical wisdom that only comes from working inside real organisations facing real constraints.

These workshops exist because of that dual perspective. They are not textbook summaries of AI, and they are not vendor-sponsored overviews of the latest platform. They are grounded in what actually works, what organisations actually struggle with, and what students actually need to compete in a world shaped by AI.

docs.title: Writing and Knowledge Sharing
docs.text:
Alongside teaching and mentoring, writing has been a consistent thread — technical writing, curriculum design, accessible explanations of difficult ideas, and public talks at events that range from industry conferences to university forums.

Sharing knowledge publicly is a commitment, not a marketing strategy.

docs.title: AI for Leaders — Let's Demystify AI
AI for Leaders — Let's Demystify AI
docs.text:
AI is reshaping industries, disrupting established business models and creating new competitive pressures. Executives and senior leaders who understand what AI actually is — rather than what the hype says it is — are the ones best positioned to make decisions that create lasting value.

This workshop cuts through the noise.

docs.title: Who This Workshop Is For
docs.text:
This workshop is designed for executives, senior managers and board members who:

  • Need to make strategic decisions about AI but lack a technical background
  • Want to evaluate AI proposals with confidence rather than relying entirely on vendors
  • Are responsible for governance, risk or accountability in their organisations
  • Are leading or sponsoring an AI adoption programme
  • Want to understand what their technical teams are actually doing

No prior technical knowledge is required. The workshop is deliberately designed for decision-makers, not data scientists.

docs.title: The Challenges This Workshop Addresses
docs.text:
Leaders routinely encounter situations where AI raises difficult questions:

  • A vendor proposes an AI solution — how do you evaluate it?
  • Your organisation wants to adopt AI at scale — where do you start?
  • Your team produces results from an AI model — how do you know if they are reliable?
  • You are asked to approve an AI governance framework — what should it contain?
  • Your competitors are moving fast — how do you move deliberately without falling behind?

This workshop builds the understanding and vocabulary needed to engage with these questions confidently.

docs.title: What Participants Will Learn
docs.text:
By the end of the workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Explain what AI is and is not, in plain language
  • Identify where AI can and cannot create genuine business value
  • Ask the right questions when evaluating AI proposals
  • Understand the conditions required for AI to scale successfully
  • Apply a practical framework for AI governance and responsible use
  • Recognise the risks of AI adoption and how to manage them
  • Lead organisational change in an AI-enabled environment
  • Establish meaningful measures of AI value

docs.title: Workshop Topics
docs.text:
Strategy & ValueScale & GovernancePeople & Change
  • AI strategy: Aligning AI initiatives with organisational goals
  • Identifying valuable use cases: How to separate genuine opportunities from noise
  • From experimentation to capability: Moving beyond pilots to sustainable AI
  • Measuring value: Defining and tracking what success actually looks like
  • Scalable AI: The conditions that allow AI to grow safely and effectively
  • Governance frameworks: Roles, responsibilities and decision rights
  • Risk and accountability: Understanding and managing what can go wrong
  • Responsible AI: Fairness, transparency, privacy and the limits of automation
  • Adoption: Why AI initiatives fail and how to avoid common traps
  • Organisational readiness: Assessing your team, data and infrastructure
  • Change management: Bringing people along rather than imposing change
  • Building internal capability: Moving from dependence to competence

docs.title: Practical Exercises
docs.text:
The workshop is interactive and discussion-led. Typical activities include:

  • Use-case evaluation: Assessing whether a proposed AI application is worth pursuing
  • Governance design: Drafting the key elements of an AI governance framework
  • Risk mapping: Identifying and prioritising AI-related risks in a given scenario
  • Value measurement: Defining meaningful success metrics for an AI initiative
  • Stakeholder simulation: Practising how to explain AI decisions to a non-technical audience

docs.title: Expected Outcomes
docs.text:
Participants leave the workshop with:

What you will take away

  • A clear, practical mental model for understanding AI
  • A framework for evaluating AI proposals and vendor claims
  • A starting structure for an AI governance approach
  • Practical tools for measuring and communicating AI value
  • Confidence to lead conversations about AI with technical and non-technical stakeholders

docs.title: Approach — How These Workshops Are Taught
Approach
docs.text:
These workshops are not lectures. They are not product demonstrations. They are not a series of slides with AI buzzwords on them.

They are structured learning experiences, built on years of teaching, mentoring and working inside real organisations — designed to help people think more clearly and act more effectively.

docs.title: Practical Rather Than Theoretical
docs.text:
Every concept introduced in these workshops is connected to a real scenario, a genuine decision or an actual challenge that organisations and individuals face.

Abstract theory has its place. But workshops for leaders and students work best when the learning is grounded in something that feels real — because it is.

Experience over abstraction

These workshops draw on experience designing nationally accredited qualifications, mentoring professionals across industry, and working at the intersection of academia and applied technology.

docs.title: Based on Real Industry Experience
docs.text:
The content of these workshops is not sourced from textbooks or vendor documentation. It comes from years of working with organisations across sectors, observing what actually works, what fails in practice, and what questions people do not know to ask until things go wrong.

That experience shapes everything: the examples used, the problems explored, the risks highlighted and the frameworks applied.

docs.title: Interactive and Discussion-Led
docs.text:
Participants are active contributors to their own learning — not passive recipients of information.

Every session includes opportunities for:

  • Discussion and debate
  • Collaborative problem-solving
  • Challenging assumptions — including the facilitator's
  • Applying frameworks to real scenarios
  • Sharing experience and perspective from within the room

The facilitator asks more questions than they answer.

docs.title: Inclusive and Accessible
docs.text:
Good education should not require people to already know the answer before they can engage with the material.

These workshops are designed to be accessible to participants who are new to AI, to data science and to formal problem-solving methods. No jargon is used without explanation. No assumption is made that participants have a technical background.

At the same time, the content is substantive enough to engage participants who do have technical backgrounds — because the skills being developed go beyond any single discipline.

docs.title: Adaptable to Different Audiences
docs.text:
The same core ideas are relevant to a board-level executive and to a high school student — but the framing, examples and activities need to be different.

Before every engagement, a brief discovery conversation ensures the workshop is designed around the specific audience: their background, their current level of understanding, their challenges and their goals.

The result is a session that feels tailored, not generic.

docs.title: Focused on Understanding, Not Product Promotion
docs.text:
These workshops have no commercial relationship with any AI vendor, platform or tool provider. No particular product is promoted. No affiliate arrangement influences the content.

The goal is to develop understanding that is durable across whatever tools exist today and whatever tools will exist in the future.

docs.title: Designed to Create Lasting Capability
docs.text:
The measure of a good workshop is not what participants say at the end. It is what they are able to do differently three months later.

These workshops aim to leave participants with:

  • Frameworks they can apply to new situations
  • Questions they know how to ask
  • Confidence to engage with AI — and AI vendors — on their own terms
  • A habit of thinking clearly before acting quickly

That is the kind of capability worth building.

docs.title: Industrial Problem-Solving Using AI & Decision Sciences
Industrial Problem-Solving Using AI & Decision Sciences
docs.text:
The world does not need more people who can use AI tools. It needs people who can define the right problem, question their assumptions, evaluate trade-offs and communicate their reasoning clearly — then choose the right tools to help.

This workshop builds those skills.

docs.title: Who This Workshop Is For
docs.text:
High School StudentsUniversity StudentsEarly-Career Professionals

Students in senior secondary school who are curious about how the technology they encounter every day actually works — and how it is used to solve genuine industrial challenges. No prior technical knowledge required.

Undergraduate and postgraduate students across engineering, science, business, mathematics and related disciplines who want to develop structured problem-solving skills that complement their academic training.

Graduates and professionals in the first few years of their careers who want to build confidence in applying systematic thinking and AI appropriately in workplace settings.

docs.title: Why Structured Problem-Solving Matters
docs.text:
Most real-world problems are poorly defined. The challenge is rarely "solve this"; it is usually "figure out what the actual problem is, and then work out whether it is worth solving and how."

AI tools can contribute enormously to this process — but only after the problem has been properly understood. Applied too early, to a poorly defined problem, AI produces outputs that are fast and confident but ultimately wrong.

Structured problem-solving is the missing ingredient. This workshop teaches it explicitly, using methods and frameworks that work in real settings.

docs.title: Design Thinking
docs.text:
Design Thinking is a human-centred approach to problem-solving that begins with understanding the people affected by a problem before reaching for a solution.

The key stages covered in the workshop:

  1. Empathise — understand the context, the people involved and what they actually need
  2. Define — articulate the problem clearly, avoiding the trap of solving the wrong thing
  3. Ideate — generate a range of possible approaches before committing to one
  4. Prototype — create quick, low-cost ways to test ideas before scaling them
  5. Test — gather real feedback and refine the approach

A common trap

Skipping directly from "problem" to "solution" is the most common mistake in applied problem-solving. Design Thinking structures the journey to avoid it.

docs.title: Decision Sciences
docs.text:
Decision Sciences provides the analytical framework for evaluating options under uncertainty — which is the condition under which most real decisions are made.

Topics covered:

  • Structuring decisions so that options can be compared fairly
  • Identifying what information matters and what does not
  • Understanding risk, probability and trade-offs
  • Using data to inform decisions — not to replace judgement
  • Recognising cognitive biases that distort decisions and how to account for them

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text:
AI is introduced as a tool within a structured problem-solving process — not as an end in itself.

Participants explore:

  • What kinds of problems AI is genuinely suited to
  • What kinds of problems AI handles poorly or dangerously
  • How to interpret AI outputs critically rather than accepting them at face value
  • How AI and human judgement work best together
  • The ethical dimensions of applying AI to real problems

docs.title: Real-World Industrial Challenges
docs.text:
The workshop uses real industrial scenarios drawn from sectors that matter: engineering, healthcare, logistics, infrastructure, energy and others.

These challenges are:

  • Complex enough to require structured thinking
  • Open-ended enough to reward creativity
  • Grounded enough in reality to feel genuinely important

Working through real challenges is more effective than studying abstract examples. Participants leave knowing what it feels like to apply these methods to something that matters.

docs.title: Team-Based Activities
docs.text:
Most of the workshop is hands-on and team-based. Groups work together to:

  • Analyse a problem and agree on what is actually being asked
  • Challenge each other's assumptions
  • Evaluate competing approaches
  • Make a reasoned recommendation they can defend

Team dynamics, communication and constructive disagreement are all part of the learning experience.

docs.title: Expected Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the workshop, participants will be able to:

Skills you will develop

  • Define the correct problem — before reaching for a solution
  • Challenge assumptions — including their own
  • Evaluate trade-offs — with limited information and under time pressure
  • Use data more thoughtfully — as evidence, not as authority
  • Apply AI appropriately — matching the tool to the problem, not the problem to the tool
  • Communicate recommendations — clearly and persuasively to different audiences
  • Build confidence — in their own reasoning and judgement
  • Career readiness — with a framework that works across roles and industries

docs.title: Understanding AI
docs.text: AI is far more than a technology trend. Understanding AI is far more important than simply using it, and that understanding begins with asking the right questions rather than chasing the latest tools.

docs.title: Curiosity Before Tools
docs.text:
Every significant advance in understanding comes from genuine curiosity — the kind that is comfortable sitting with a question rather than rushing to an answer.

The AI landscape is full of tools. New models, platforms and frameworks arrive faster than anyone can evaluate them. The organisations and individuals who navigate this landscape well are not the ones with the most tools. They are the ones with the sharpest questions.

Before reaching for a new tool, it is worth asking:

  • What problem am I actually trying to solve?
  • What does success look like, and how will I know when I have achieved it?
  • What assumptions am I making, and have I tested them?

docs.title: Understanding Before Adoption
docs.text:
Adoption without understanding creates fragility. Organisations that adopt AI because competitors are doing it — or because a vendor made a compelling presentation — often find themselves with impressive technology and disappointing results.

Understanding what AI can and cannot do, where it is reliable and where it introduces risk, and what conditions are needed for it to create genuine value: these are the foundations of effective adoption.

A useful test

Before committing to an AI solution, ask: could we explain to a sceptical board member — in plain language — why this approach is the right one for this problem? If the answer is no, more understanding is needed before more adoption.

docs.title: Better Questions Before Faster Answers
docs.text:
Speed is seductive. AI can produce answers faster than any human could. But a fast answer to the wrong question is worse than a slow answer to the right one.

The discipline of asking better questions is not instinctive. It requires practice, intellectual honesty, and the willingness to go back and re-examine assumptions that felt solid.

This is one of the core skills developed in these workshops — not how to use a particular tool, but how to approach a problem in a way that produces answers worth having.

docs.title: Responsible Use
docs.text:
AI systems are not neutral. They encode assumptions, reflect the data they were trained on, and produce outputs that can cause real harm if applied carelessly.

Responsible use is not a compliance checkbox. It is an ongoing practice of asking:

  • Who could be affected by this system?
  • What could go wrong, and how likely is that?
  • How will we detect problems, and how will we respond?
  • Who is accountable when something goes wrong?

These questions do not slow down good work. They are the difference between good work and work that merely looks good until it fails publicly.

docs.title: Human Judgement
docs.text:
AI systems augment human capability. They do not replace human judgement — and in situations that matter most, they should not be allowed to.

Understanding the boundary between what AI can reliably handle and what requires human decision-making is one of the most important skills for leaders and practitioners alike.

This is not technophobia. It is appropriate caution, applied thoughtfully.

docs.title: Measurable Impact
docs.text:
AI that creates genuine value creates measurable value. Not value that can be described in general terms, but value that can be traced to specific outcomes: decisions made faster, errors reduced, capacity freed, opportunities identified that would otherwise have been missed.

If the impact of an AI initiative cannot be measured, that is worth examining. Either the problem definition needs sharpening, or the initiative is not as valuable as it appears.
